channel.title: NPR Programs: Morning Edition
channel.description: Morning Edition takes listeners around the country and the world with multi-faceted stories and commentaries every weekday. Hosts Steve Inskeep, Leila Fadel, Michel Martin and A Martínez bring you the latest breaking news and features to prepare you for the day.

item.title: U.S. employers add only 29,000 jobs in September, much less than August
item.description: The Labor Department offered an update Friday on the strength of the U.S. job market. The news comes as long-term interest rates have been climbing.

item.title: Economist discusses high bond yields and the September jobs report
item.description: NPR's Michel Martin speaks to Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, about high bond yields and the September jobs report.

item.title: Dance Theatre of Harlem returns to Africa for first time in 3 decades
item.description: NPR's Michel Martin speaks with Robert Garland, artistic director of the Dance Theatre of Harlem, a company where he was once principal dancer and that he is taking back to the African continent for the first time since the 1990s.

item.title: Car crimes in San Francisco have dropped. The city says Flock cameras have helped
item.description: Car crimes have plunged in San Francisco over the last four years. The city credits, in part, Flock cameras. We investigate the claim.

item.title: Weakening of the Voter Rights Act has charged a surge in Black voters
item.description: Since the 2024 election, Black voters have led a surge in Democratic voter enthusiasm by responding to a Supreme Court decision that weakened the Voting Rights Act.

item.title: Some school districts switch to electric buses as diesel prices soar
item.description: School districts that drive long distances are navigating record high diesel prices in different ways. Some have transitioned to electric or propane buses to ease the pinch.

item.title: Tennessee governor pauses executions after Christa Pike survives 2 lethal injections
item.description: Reaction was swift after the execution of a Tennessee woman was halted because she survived two lethal injections.
